title: How To Improve Classroom Behavior In One Lesson -lesson/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin introduces the 'how not' strategy, which he calls a close cousin of detailed modeling: after demonstrating a procedure correctly, the teacher also acts out, with exaggerated humor, how the procedure is typically done incorrectly. Using lining up for lunch as an example, he explains how a teacher can enlist students to play the correct-behaving line while the teacher hams up common failures like leaving a chair out, talking, cutting, or pushing. He argues the strategy's power comes from its entertainment value and from making poor behavior look genuinely absurd, comparing the desired classroom mindset to the shocked reaction of museum-goers when someone cuts a line. Because students find the exaggerated demonstration memorable and slightly embarrassing to be associated with, he claims few will repeat the modeled misbehavior afterward.
points: The 'how not' strategy builds on detailed modeling by also exaggeratedly demonstrating how a procedure is commonly done wrong.
Humor and exaggeration make the demonstration memorable, so students are less likely to repeat the modeled misbehavior out of embarrassment.
Framing poor behavior as socially absurd, similar to line-cutting at a museum, shifts how students perceive misbehavior.
The strategy requires prior familiarity with the class's typical failure points so the teacher can model realistic, recognizable mistakes.
quotes: The “how not” strategy is so powerful because it clarifies for students exactly what unacceptable behavior looks like, and they’ll immediately recognize it. In fact, when you use this strategy, you’ll find your students laughing and nodding their heads knowingly.
The more you exaggerate the unwanted behavior, the more memorable it will be for your students.

In fact, they’ll never forget it. And few will behave in the way you modeled ever again. They’ll be embarrassed to. The “how not” strategy works so well because it points out the absurdity of poor behavior.

I was at a museum in Europe several years ago, waiting in line to see an exhibit, and a man and a woman cut in line, positioning themselves near the front. Those of us behind were astounded at their rudeness and demanded they go to the end of the line.
Allow your students to see what their poor behavior looks like and how it affects others, and it will hit home like no other classroom management strategy.
